explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The prophecy asks why she's crying aloud, then says anguish grips her like a woman in labor (Micah 4:9). It's a picture of pain that comes in waves and can't be ignored. I once got stuck in a stamper rack and thought THAT was pain. It was not even close.

That's a sad picture, baker, but it isn't the one Micah uses. The prophecy says anguish grips her like a woman in labor (Micah 4:9). No widow shows up in these verses. Keep your eyes on the labor, because it comes back in this passage.

Good thinking, baker, because the Bible does use that picture elsewhere. Jesus saw the crowds as “…like sheep without a shepherd.” (Matthew 9:36). But in Micah 4:9 the comparison is a woman in labor. Hold onto the shepherd idea, because one shows up later in this passage.

Yes, baker. The text says, “there you will be rescued; there the LORD will redeem you from the hand of your enemies!” (Micah 4:10). Babylon is the last place you'd expect a rescue to happen. It's like finding your keys in the one coat pocket you checked three times. The LORD does the redeeming, and He does it right there.

This one is actually true, baker. Micah 4:10 says, “there you will be rescued; there the LORD will redeem you from the hand of your enemies!” The word "there" is doing the work, and it points to Babylon. I know Babylon sounds like the end of the road, but the text puts the redeeming right in that spot.

Not quite, baker. The text says the opposite: the nations "do not know the thoughts of the LORD or understand His plan" (Micah 4:12). They're busy saying what they want to do to Zion. They have no idea what the LORD is doing. So the answer is False.

Right, baker. Micah 4:12 says they do not know the thoughts of the LORD or understand His plan. They gathered with their own plan in mind, saying “Let her be defiled…” (Micah 4:11). It's like showing up to a surprise party thinking you're the guest list. The LORD's plan was a different one.

You got it, baker. The text says, “Rise and thresh, O Daughter of Zion” (Micah 4:13). Threshing is hard work, so this is a call to get up and move. The nations may think they came to stare, but Zion is told to stand and work.

Close, but no bowing here, baker. The message to the Daughter of Zion is “Rise and thresh” (Micah 4:13). Rising is the opposite of bowing down. She's told to get up, and the LORD says He'll give her horns of iron and hooves of bronze.

I get it, baker. When a crowd gathers against you, running sounds smart. I'd be out the door with my hat in my mustache. But Micah 4:13 says, “Rise and thresh, O Daughter of Zion.” No running is mentioned.

Yes, baker. The text says, “Then you will devote their gain to the LORD, their wealth to the Lord of all the earth.” (Micah 4:13). The wealth gets handed over, not hoarded. It all goes to the One who is Lord of all the earth.

Tempting, baker, but the text says something else. Micah 4:13 says she will devote their gain to the LORD and their wealth to the Lord of all the earth. Nothing in it is kept back for her. It's all set apart for Him.

That would be a surprise ending, baker, but it's not in the text. Micah 4:13 says she will devote their gain to the LORD, their wealth to the Lord of all the earth. The wealth goes to the LORD. It doesn't go back to the peoples.

Perfect, baker. The text says, “But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel” (Micah 5:2). A small town gets named, and the ruler comes out of it. It's small on the map and big in what's promised.

Good guess, baker, but that's not the town Micah names. Micah 5:2 says, “But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah…” The ruler comes out of Bethlehem Ephrathah. That's the name to remember.
Tekoa is a real town, baker. The prophet Amos came from there (Amos 1:1). But Micah 5:2 names a different small town: Bethlehem Ephrathah. That's where the ruler over Israel comes from.

You got it, baker. The text says this ruler's origins are “of old, from the days of eternity” (Micah 5:2). The town is small, but His origins go all the way back. That's a lot of history for one little place to carry.

explanations.answer: From the days of King Saul
explanations.explanation: Saul was Israel's first king (1 Samuel 10:1), so that's a good long way back, baker. But Micah 5:2 goes much further. It says the ruler's origins are “of old, from the days of eternity.” Saul's days don't come close.

explanations.answer: From the days of the judges
explanations.explanation: The judges were leaders the LORD raised up before Israel had kings (Judges 2:16). That's old, baker, but Micah goes back further still. Micah 5:2 says this ruler's origins are “from the days of eternity.” No judge's days can reach that far.

Yes, baker. The text says, “then the rest of His brothers will return to the children of Israel” (Micah 5:3). It happens after she who is in labor has given birth. Returning means people coming back, and that's the picture here.
I see why you'd go there with a ruler in the picture, baker. But Micah 5:3 doesn't say bow. It says the rest of His brothers will return to the children of Israel. The word is return.
Close, baker, but the verse doesn't have them talking. Micah 5:3 says the rest of His brothers will return to the children of Israel. This is about people coming back. The word that fits is return.

That's right, baker. The text says, “He will stand and shepherd His flock in the strength of the LORD” (Micah 5:4). The strength behind the shepherding comes from the LORD. This ruler isn't doing it on His own power.

This one is true, baker. Micah 5:4 says, “He will stand and shepherd His flock in the strength of the LORD, in the majestic name of the LORD His God.” The strength is the LORD's. So the statement matches the text.
You got it, baker. The text says, “And they will dwell securely” (Micah 5:4). A shepherd standing over the flock means the flock can settle down. Nobody has to keep one eye on the door.
I can see the thinking, baker, since the flock has been through a lot. But Micah 5:4 says the opposite: “And they will dwell securely.” With this shepherd, they stay put.
That's how it sounds when a siege is in the news, baker. But Micah 5:4 says, “And they will dwell securely.” Living securely means staying in the open without fear. Hiding isn't in the picture.

That's a keeper, baker. Micah says, “And He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land and tramples our citadels.” (Micah 5:5). Assyria is the invading nation in Micah's day. The ruler doesn't just bring peace. He IS the peace.
A lookout sounds sensible when an army's coming, baker. But Micah 5:5 says, “He will be our peace.” The word is peace, not lookout.
A banner is a good thing to rally behind, baker, but that's not the word. Micah 5:5 says the ruler will be our peace when Assyria invades. Peace is what fits in the blank.

Not quite, baker. Micah doesn't have them running anywhere. He says, “And they will rule the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod with the blade drawn.” (Micah 5:6). They hold the ground and rule it. So the answer is False.

You got it, baker. Micah 5:6 says, “And they will rule the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod with the blade drawn.” Ruling a land is the opposite of fleeing it. The verse ends with this line: “So He will deliver us…”
